newsitem.title: USA: Simpson jury urged to set heavy punitive damages.
newsitem.headline: Simpson jury urged to set heavy punitive damages.

text.p: The plaintiffs in O.J. Simpson's civil trial on Thursday urged jurors to punish him by imposing heavy damages for the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend on top of $8.5 million they already awarded.

Daniel Petrocelli, the plaintiffs' lead attorney, said Simpson had violated the rights of the victims in taking their lives, adding, "We are not just talking about any violations, we are talking about the most unconscionable violations."
The jury on Tuesday blamed Simpson for the June 12, 1994, murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman and ordered him to pay $8.5 million in compensatory damages.
The former football star, who was acquitted on criminal murder charges in 1995, was absent from the courtroom on Thursday as the four-month trial entered its final phase.

Attorney John Kelly, who represents the estate of Nicole Brown Simpson, told the panel that by imposing substantial punitive damages it could ensure that "no man, especially a man of fame and fortune, will ever again act with such reckless disregard for human life as Mr. Simpson did."

But Simpson's attorney, Robert Baker, argued that Simpson had been punished enough and urged jurors to award "zero punitive damages," saying to do otherwise would amount to "piling on and attempting to destroy Mr. Simpson."
Baker said Simpson had no assets and owed lawyers and mortgage payments. "He has no equity in his home, he has no savings," he added.

In assessing punitive damages, jurors will be instructed by the judge to base their decision on how reprehensible the crime was and how much the award would hurt Simpson financially. The jury's first round of deliberations yielded a surprisingly large award of compensatory damages, which will be paid entirely to Goldman's family members for the loss of his love, companionship and moral support.

In this round, they will determine punitive damages, designed to punish Simpson for his actions and set an example for society. But the jurors, who may begin deliberations by the end of the day, were presented with an array of conflicting figures about Simpson's wealth or lack of it.
His financial statements indicated that at the end of last year he had a negative net worth of more than $800,000, meaning his debts were greater than his assets.

Baker told the jurors that taking into account Tuesday's $8.5 million judgment against him, Simpson now had a negative net worth of more than $9 million. In addition, he said Simpson could no longer make money by selling his name and signing autographs.

But Neill Freeman, an accountant and financial investigator testifying for the plaintiffs, strongly disagreed with Simpson's estimate of his worth and his future earning powers. Freeman accused Simpson of overstating his liabilities and understating his assets in "incomplete" financial information given to the plaintiffs.

Far from being broke, Freeman said, Simpson had a net worth of more than $15.7 million as of Dec. 31, 1996. In addition, he said he had calculated Simpson's future earning potential for the rest of his life at about $24.9 million from selling his "name and likeness" in the form of product endorsements and autograph signing.
Marketing experts say that while Simpson is unlikely to earn money from such enterprises in the United States he is still a big draw abroad.

Freeman said he had discovered that in 1996 Simpson received $1.75 million from his insurance company for legal costs and a further $1.25 million from a food processing company he has investments in for a total of $3 million.
But during that period Freeman said he could find no evidence that Simpson had paid off any debts. "I don't understand where the cash went," he said.
Freeman said among Simpson's current assets was $4.1 million in two pension funds, but Baker countered that his client could not access that money for five years.
